lead: Every structure has natural frequencies at which it prefers to vibrate. A wing, a tailplane or a skin panel that is struck rings at these frequencies, and its damping decides how quickly the motion dies out. In flight the airflow over a deforming wing changes the air loads, and the air loads change the deformation: that interaction is aeroelasticity. At one speed a wing can twist without limit, which is divergence; at another it can oscillate with growing amplitude, which is flutter. This chapter builds the one-degree-of-freedom vibration model, reduces a wing to it, and uses it to explain divergence and flutter.
prereq: You need: Newton's second law, beam bending stiffness EI, and lift and pitching moment on an aerofoil.

sections.h3: One degree of freedom: mass, spring and damper

blocks.text: Take a mass m (kg) on a spring of stiffness k (N/m) with a viscous damper c (N·s/m), displaced by x(t) (m) and driven by a force F(t). Newton's law gives m ẍ + c ẋ + k x = F(t). With no force and no damping the mass oscillates for ever at its natural frequency:

blocks.where: ω<sub>n</sub> is the undamped natural frequency (rad/s); f<sub>n</sub> the same in Hz; ζ the damping ratio (dimensionless); c<sub>c</sub> = 2√(km) the critical damping (N·s/m).

blocks.text: Damping sets the character of free motion. ζ < 1 is underdamped: the mass oscillates at ω<sub>d</sub> = ω<sub>n</sub>√(1 − ζ²) while the motion dies away. ζ = 1 is critically damped: the fastest return with no overshoot. ζ > 1 is overdamped: a slow return with no oscillation. Aircraft structures are lightly damped, with ζ of a few per cent.
Under a harmonic force F₀ sin Ωt the steady response has amplitude X, which depends on the frequency ratio r = Ω/ω<sub>n</sub>:

blocks.where: X is the amplitude (m); F₀/k the static deflection under F₀ (m); r = Ω/ω<sub>n</sub>. At r = 1, X = F₀/(2ζk).

blocks.text: Near r = 1 the response peaks: resonance. The peak is 1/(2ζ) times the static deflection, so a structure with ζ = 0.02 responds 25 times more at resonance than to a steady force of the same size. That is why engine, propeller and rotor frequencies are kept away from the structure's natural frequencies.

sections.h3: Reducing a wing to a lumped model

blocks.text: A real wing has distributed mass and stiffness, so it has many natural frequencies, each with a mode shape in which all points move in step: first bending, first torsion, second bending and so on. For a hand estimate, assume a shape φ(x) for one mode and let the wing move as w(x, t) = φ(x) q(t). Kinetic and strain energy then reduce the wing to one mass and one spring for the coordinate q:
M = ∫ μ φ² dx,   K = ∫ EI (φ″)² dx,   ω² = K/M
blocks.where: M is the generalised mass (kg); K the generalised stiffness (N/m); μ the mass per unit length (kg/m); EI the bending stiffness (N·m²); φ″ the second derivative of the assumed shape; the integrals run over the span.

blocks.text: This is Rayleigh's method. The assumed shape must meet the support conditions (for a cantilever, zero deflection and slope at the root). Any such shape gives a frequency at or above the true one, because a wrong shape is effectively a stiffer structure, so the lowest estimate is the best. A softer laminate, a heavier fuel load or a longer span all lower ω.

Divergence is static. Take a wing section whose aerodynamic centre lies a distance e ahead of its flexural axis, held by a torsional stiffness K_θ (N·m/rad). Lift L = q S a₁(α₀ + θ) acts at the aerodynamic centre, so it twists the section nose up by θ, which raises the lift further. Moment balance about the flexural axis gives K_θθ = q S e a₁(α₀ + θ), so θ = q S e a₁α₀/(K_θ − q S e a₁). The twist grows without limit as the denominator reaches zero:

blocks.where: q<sub>D</sub> is the divergence dynamic pressure (N/m²); e the distance of the aerodynamic centre ahead of the flexural axis (m); S the wing area of the section (m²); a₁ = dC_L/dα the lift-curve slope (per rad); V<sub>D</sub> the divergence speed (m/s); ρ the air density (kg/m³).

blocks.text: Below divergence the twist is magnified by 1/(1 − q/q<sub>D</sub>). Moving the flexural axis forward (smaller e) or stiffening the wing in torsion raises V<sub>D</sub>. A swept-back wing bends in a way that reduces its angle of attack and rarely diverges; forward sweep does the opposite.

Flutter is dynamic. The bending and torsion modes of a wing couple through the unsteady air loads, which lag behind the motion. Above the flutter speed the air feeds more energy into the oscillation each cycle than the structural damping removes: the effective damping becomes negative and the amplitude grows. Flutter can occur below the divergence speed, so both must be shown to lie beyond the flight envelope. Mass balance ahead of the flexural axis and high torsional stiffness raise the flutter speed. How strongly the air loads lag is set by the reduced frequency k<sub>r</sub> = ωb/V, with b the semi-chord (m), ω the frequency (rad/s) and V the airspeed (m/s): small k<sub>r</sub> means nearly steady air loads, large k<sub>r</sub> strong lag.

figure.caption: The first worked example: steady amplitude of the 500 kg, 200 kN/m model under a 1 kN force against frequency ratio. The static deflection is 5 mm; at resonance (r = 1) the amplitude is 12.5 mm, 1/(2ζ) = 2.5 times larger for ζ = 0.2, and at r = 2 it has fallen to 1.61 mm. Halving the damping (dashed) doubles the peak.

spec.aria: A graph of amplitude X in millimetres against frequency ratio r from 0 to 3. The solid curve for damping ratio 0.2 starts at 5 millimetres at r equal to 0, rises to a peak of 12.5 millimetres at r equal to 1, and falls to 1.61 millimetres at r equal to 2. A dashed curve for damping ratio 0.1 rises much higher near r equal to 1 and leaves the top of the graph.

examples.question: A wing model has mass m = 500 kg, stiffness k = 200 kN/m and damping c = 4000 N·s/m. Find ω<sub>n</sub>, f<sub>n</sub>, ζ and the damped frequency. For a force of amplitude 1 kN, find the static deflection and the resonant amplitude.
steps: At resonance: X = F₀/(2ζk) = 1000/(2 × 0.20 × 200,000) = 12.5 mm, 2.5 times the static value. Check with the general formula at r = 1: 12.5 mm; at r = 2 it falls to 1.61 mm.
examples.answer: ω<sub>n</sub> = 20 rad/s, f<sub>n</sub> = 3.18 Hz, ζ = 0.20, ω<sub>d</sub> = 19.6 rad/s; static 5 mm, resonant 12.5 mm.

examples.question: A wing is modelled as a uniform cantilever 6 m long with EI = 5 × 10⁶ N·m² and μ = 50 kg/m. Estimate its first bending frequency by Rayleigh's method with φ = 1 − cos(πx/2L), and compare with the exact 3.516√(EI/μL⁴). Then a wing section with K_θ = 200 kN·m/rad, e = 0.15 m, S = 4 m² and a₁ = 5.7 per rad flies at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³). Find its divergence speed.
steps: The shape has φ = 0 and φ′ = 0 at the root x = 0, as a cantilever needs. φ″ = (π/2L)² cos(πx/2L).
K = EI (π/2L)⁴ ∫₀ᴸ cos²(πx/2L) dx = EI (π/2L)⁴ L/2 = (π⁴/32) EI/L³ = 3.044 EI/L³.
M = μ ∫₀ᴸ [1 − cos(πx/2L)]² dx = μL(3/2 − 4/π) = 0.2268 μL.
Exact: 3.516 × 8.784 = 30.9 rad/s (4.92 Hz). Rayleigh is 4.2% high, as it must be.
V<sub>D</sub> = √(2 × 58,480/1.225) = 309 m/s. At half this dynamic pressure the twist from any initial incidence is already doubled.
examples.answer: ω ≈ 32.2 rad/s by Rayleigh (30.9 rad/s exact); V<sub>D</sub> = 309 m/s.

traps: Reporting ω<sub>n</sub> in rad/s as a frequency in Hz. 20 rad/s is 3.18 Hz.
Writing ζ = c/√(km). Critical damping is 2√(km).
Calling divergence flutter. Divergence is a static loss of torsional stiffness with no oscillation; flutter is a growing oscillation.
Taking a Rayleigh estimate as a lower bound. Any admissible shape gives a frequency at or above the true one.
Putting e behind the flexural axis into q<sub>D</sub> = K_θ/(eSa₁). Divergence needs the aerodynamic centre ahead of the flexural axis; if it lies behind, the section does not diverge.

quiz.q: Define natural frequency and damping ratio of a one-degree-of-freedom system and state the three damping cases.
quiz.a: ω<sub>n</sub> = √(k/m), the frequency of free undamped motion; ζ = c/(2√(km)). ζ < 1 underdamped (decaying oscillation), ζ = 1 critically damped, ζ > 1 overdamped (no oscillation).

quiz.q: A mass of 200 kg on a spring of 80 kN/m has damping 1600 N·s/m. Find ω<sub>n</sub>, f<sub>n</sub> and ζ.
A wing oscillates at 30 rad/s; its semi-chord is 1.5 m and the airspeed 150 m/s. Find the reduced frequency.
Why does Rayleigh's method always give a frequency at or above the true one?
quiz.a: Forcing the structure into an assumed shape is like adding constraints, which can only stiffen it. The true mode is the shape that makes K/M smallest, so any other admissible shape gives a larger ω.

quiz.q: Distinguish divergence from flutter, and say which design changes raise each speed.
quiz.a: Divergence is static: at q<sub>D</sub> the aerodynamic twisting moment grows as fast as the torsional stiffness resists, and the twist runs away without oscillation. It is raised by torsional stiffness and by moving the flexural axis forward. Flutter is dynamic coupling of bending and torsion through lagging air loads, with negative net damping; it is raised by torsional stiffness, mass balance forward and separating the bending and torsion frequencies.

quiz.q: In the divergence example the flexural axis is moved 5 cm forward. Find the new divergence speed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Flutter clearance uses unsteady panel aerodynamics with the p-k method, ground vibration tests to measure the modes, and flight flutter tests. Composite wings use bend–twist coupling from laminate design to raise divergence and flutter speeds. Search for p-k flutter method and ground vibration test.
